newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Pugnacious Kohl vows to run again in 1998.
newsitem.headline: Pugnacious Kohl vows to run again in 1998.

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl cheered his party and coalition partners on Thursday with a surprise announcement that he planned to stand for re-election in 1998 for an unprecedented fifth term.

Kohl, celebrating his 67th birthday and under pressure from economic ills as never before in his 14-year tenure, said he felt an obligation to run again in the next general election in late 1998 because of the challenges Germany faced.

In an interview with ARD national television during his Easter holiday in the Austrian resort of Bad Hofgastein, Kohl said he wanted to play a role in NATO's expansion, European integration and the launch of a European Union single currency.
With his typical sense of political theatre, Kohl delivered a pugnacious performance with much of the determination and drive which even party colleagues have missed in recent months.
"I will stand again because I believe I have an obligation to do this in the current situation," he said. "I want to pursue the necessary reforms. I want this country to have a future."

The news put an end to speculation that Kohl no longer had the stomach to face soaring unemployment, the need for painful welfare cuts to meet the criteria for European monetary union, and the challenge of instituting long-delayed structural reform.

The man seen as Kohl's most likely successor, Christian Democrat (CDU) parliamentary leader Wolfgang Schaeuble, said that "especially in a time of difficult social upheavals, important political decisions and significant foreign policy changes, Germany needs a chancellor with authority and the ability to get things done".

There was relief too from Kohl's coalition partners, the centrist Free Democrats and the Bavarian Christian Social Union, who had been urging him to declare his candidacy early to rally support in the coalition and put pressure on the opposition SPD.

Kohl, already post-war Germany's longest-serving chancellor, took office in 1982 and has defeated four SPD challengers since then. Only Count Otto von Bismarck, who was chancellor for 19 years and two months in the 19th century, has held power longer.

But his failure this year to marshal party and coalition decisively behind major tax and pensions reform projects, and above all a rise in unemployment to its highest level since 1933, have put the opposition well ahead in opinion polls.
Kohl gave short shrift to suggestions from the interviewers that his reforms had failed.
He was adamant that Germany had the ability to solve its problems, telling them: "The world is not coming to an end. It goes on, and in pretty good order, even for the Germans."
Kohl said Germany was trying to push through within months a tax reform which would take years elsewhere.
He insisted that unemployment would start to fall this year once the fruits were felt of recent government measures to cut the tax burden on companies and reduce non-wage costs.
And he brushed aside scepticism over Germany's ability, in the face of high unemployment, to cut its budget deficit far enough to qualify for monetary union.
"What the gurus say is fine but the gurus don't make decisions," he said. "We are having difficulty, but we are going to make it."

Kohl's long hesitation about whether to stand again had led to speculation that he would wait until he was sure his reforms could be pushed through and unemployment could be tackled before committing himself.
Opinion polls suggest, however, that he still has some way to go to convince fellow citizens he has done the right mix.
In an unrepresentative poll of 60,000 viewers who called the private television station RTL, 67.5 percent said Kohl should not stand again against 32.5 percent who said he should.
